bodyText: When extraordinary weather is on the way, people reach for amped-up language to communicate the scale of the hazard. But finding the right word to match that danger is like trying to find the right shoe size, Vurdelja said. The language can be too small, minimizing the threat, or it can be too big - exaggerations that can lead to nihilism or desensitization. It's extremely important that the word communicates the seriousness, the magnitude, the severity of the event itself

title: 证据累积：气候变化可能正在增强厄尔尼诺事件
originalTitle: Evidence builds showing climate change could be intensifying El Niño events
bodyText: As a potentially historic El Niño builds in the Pacific, evidence suggests that climate change is ratcheting up the intensity of such events. And as temperatures rise in the future, the number and frequency of strong El Niños could increase even further, some experts say. The 2026-2027 event is clearly going to be very large, up there with the handful of largest events that we're aware of, Cane said. A pre-print study found an event of this size is six times more likely due to climate change. In 2024, an El Niño year, global average temperatures reached 1.55 C (2.79 F) above pre-industrial levels, according to the World Meteorological Organization. In 1982, a marine heatwave triggered by a very strong El Niño killed off around 95% of the coral in the Galapagos.

title: 德国为美国气候数据建方舟：汉堡存储中心与 3500 万美元预算
originalTitle: Why Germany is building an ark for US climate data
bodyText: The U.S. government quit both the U.N. Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, or IPCC, and the U.N. Framework Convention on Climate Change in January, though U.S. researchers are still contributing to global climate science. To support them, the German Research Foundation in late 2025 set up a program, with a budget of $35 million, to provide a safe haven for permanently storing copies of U.S. climate data. In a modern five-story building in the center of Hamburg, Germany, technicians are preparing to install several new racks - gray metal casings that hold computing hardware - alongside the scores that already line the narrow, dimly lit corridors of the German Climate Computing Center, or DKRZ, one of the world's largest repositories for climate simulation data. The DKRZ project is called CMIP7-ark - a lifeboat for the U.S. contribution to the seventh IPCC assessment.

bodyText: Videos show a large landslide on the Kaligandaki River at Lete in Mustang. On 27 September 2026, a large landslide occurred on the Kaligandaki River in Nepal. The landslide, which was triggered by heavy rainfall over the last few days, has been widely shared on social media. The location is reported to be Lete, although this is difficult to pin down. It appears to be in the area of [28.63113, 83.61219], although this is speculation. The landslide appears to have been valley-blocking, but news reports suggest that the breach event occurred within a short period, minimising the hazard. There is some uncertainty as to whether this landslide caused loss of life. At present, it does not appear on the Bipad portal as a mass fatality event.

title: 全球城市因地下水超采沉降：雅加达年降 10 厘米，天津 1500 万人受威胁
originalTitle: Cities across the world are sinking because of groundwater depletion, but the process can be reversed
bodyText: Land subsidence, the gradual sinking of the ground surface, affects many of the world's major cities. Parts of Jakarta, the capital of Indonesia, are sinking more than 10 centimeters (4 inches) each year, prompting the government to plan a relocation of the city. The coastal city of Tianjin, China, is home to 15 million people. It, too, is a subsidence hotspot. If sinking there continues unabated, 15% of the city could be at risk of flooding by 2050. Groundwater depletion is the main driver: when water is pumped from aquifers, the pore pressure that supports the overlying sediment drops and the ground compacts.

title: 姑里雅冰帽复钻冰芯把高原冰记录推到 12.8 万年
originalTitle: Digging deep, researchers find high-altitude glacier endured last ice age
bodyText: Ice cores recovered from an ice cap in northwestern Tibet appear to preserve fragments of ancient ice from the last ice age, extending Earth's glacial record by more than 100,000 years and making them the oldest ice cores ever recovered from the region, according to a new study. The analysis, comparing ice cores drilled from the Guliya Plateau in 1992 and 2015, shows that both samples contained similar oxygen isotope patterns, suggesting that the environmental signals they contain are consistent and reproducible. Researchers take samples from the Guliya Plateau inside of a core drilling dome in 2015. Credit: The Ohio State University. To measure the true age of the ice, researchers employed advanced dating techniques to detect two radioactive isotopes, beryllium and chlorine. The team used these elements to mark the Laschamp geomagnetic excursion, more than 41,000 years ago. Outside of the polar regions, this is the only ice core we have from the mountaintops that goes back that far, Thompson said.

title: 美东东北气旋风暴潮：拉瑞坦湾与特拉华湾最高
originalTitle: Why the nor'easter's storm surge was so high, and what it says about the El Nino winter ahead
bodyText: As a powerful nor'easter hit the U.S. Atlantic coast in late September 2026, the ocean poured into coastal neighborhoods from North Carolina to New York. Water from the storm surge and heavy rain filled streets and surrounded homes as near-hurricane-force winds knocked out power. Storm surge is the piling up of water caused by strong winds pushing water onshore. There are four basic factors that determine the surge height at any given location: the strength of the onshore wind, the size of the storm, the shape of the coastline and the depth of the ocean. The September 2026 surge was highest where the water was directed into shallow bays and inlets. Some of the largest surges during the nor'easter were in Raritan Bay in New Jersey and Delaware Bay. The slow movement of the nor'easter up the East Coast resulted in a large, sustained surge. A computer model forecasts the nor'easter's winds in late September 2026. Credit: Brian Tang, NOAA images.

title: 奔赴“县”场｜安徽黟县：如何从“到此一游”到“留此成邻”
bodyText: 县城，盛得下梦想，载得动乡愁。一到假期，年轻人“奔县”成风潮。今年国庆，澎湃新闻记者奔赴“县”场，感受中国县域的生机、韧性与真实生活。这里既有县域产业突围、文旅融合的鲜活探索，也有古老文脉在小城焕发新生的转型实践。今天，我们关注安徽黟县。我们坐车从黄山北站出来，沿新铺的旅游公路往黟县碧阳镇石亭村走。路旁指示牌上依次写着“西递”“宏村”“碧山”。每个指示牌背后，都是全国知名的景区与旅游目的地。县城不过七万多本地人，一年却接待1900多万外地游客。走访里，我们深刻感受到一套文旅产品正在这个小县城悄然迭代：从“看房子”到“做鱼灯”，从“到此一游”到“留此成邻”。黟县，或许能为中国县域文旅经济提供一种样本。
